http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/tehra.text: Hossein Taeb, the cleric who commanded the Basij during the 2009 crackdown on the Green Movement and led the Revolutionary Guards' intelligence service for 13 years, has been reappointed as head of the IRGC's militia.The decision to bring back one of the Islamic Republic's most senior internal security figures to a frontline position in the early months of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei's rule is part of a recent reshuffle among the Islamic Republic's political, military and security elites.The appointment signals that the Tehran regime's new leadership is preparing for possible unrest at home, amid the ongoing war with the US and mounting economic pressure from sanctions.Who is Hossein Taeb?Taeb joined the IRGC as a teenager and later served in the Ministry of Intelligence before returning to the Guards.He became Basij commander in July 2008, less than a year before Iran's disputed presidential election triggered the mass demonstrations of June 2009 known as the Green Movement.The Basij played a central role in the crackdown that followed. The US sanctioned Taeb in 2010 over his command responsibility for the violence, with the EU following suit in 2011.In late 2009, he was appointed the first head of the newly created IRGC Intelligence Organisation.He held that position for roughly 13 years, during which the body became one of the country's most powerful security institutions, at times competing with and frequently overshadowing the civilian Ministry of Intelligence.Under his tenure, the organisation expanded into cases involving political opponents, journalists, environmental activists and dual nationals.The most prominent operation associated with his time as IRGC intelligence chief was the capture and extradition of Ruhollah Zam, an Iranian dissident living in France who ran the popular Telegram channel Amad News.The IRGC brought Zam to Iran in 2019. He was executed in 2020.Taeb was replaced in June 2022 by Mohammad Kazemi and moved to an advisory role under the IRGC commander.His removal followed a period of significant intelligence failures, including operations attributed to Israel that exposed serious weaknesses in Iran's counter-intelligence.These included alleged penetrations of sensitive sites and the killing of nuclear scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh in November 2020 outside Tehran.Iranian authorities never publicly confirmed those failures as the reason for his departure.Taeb was not expelled from the security establishment, but was instead moved directly into another senior position.Taeb and Mojtaba Khamenei are reported to have longstanding ties dating back to the Iran-Iraq War, during which both were associated with the Habib battalion of the IRGC's 27th Mohammad Rasulollah Division.Networks formed at the time later became significant pathways to institutional advancement within Iran's security structure for the most loyal cadre.His return to the Basij under Mojtaba Khamenei's leadership, rather than his retirement after the 2022 setback, suggests those ties remain close.Why the Basij mattersThe Basij maintains a presence in neighbourhoods, places of worship, universities and government offices and has been used to monitor citizens and communities, mobilise regime support and suppress protests.The order appointing Taeb emphasised expanding the Basij's "popular intelligence network," improving training and integrating new technologies — language that points to Tehran's renewed interest in its domestic surveillance.Placing a veteran intelligence official in charge of the Basij could allow the force to shift from a body deployed reactively after protests erupt to one embedded in a broader system that detects and contains dissent before it spreads.The choice of Taeb — who has moved from one top position to another within the security apparatus over four decades without being permanently removed from the establishment's core — also indicates that the IRGC, an elite paramilitary corps that answers directly to the ayatollah, remains crucial to decision-making in Tehran.Former president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad publicly accused him in 2018 of fabricating cases against political opponents, in a rare public dispute over power between the presidency and the IRGC intelligence apparatus.During Hassan Rouhani's presidency, the IRGC intelligence service under Taeb openly challenged the civilian Ministry of Intelligence in several high-profile cases, in another shift in security and political power toward institutions directly linked to the ayatollah.

Photograph: Pablo Martínez Monsiváis/AP Trump administration Ex-CIA director John Brennan subpoenaed in Trump ‘grand conspiracy’ investigation Subpoena is among a flurry issued in recent weeks as part of DoJ inquiry into alleged conspiracy against Trump Associated Press Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.52 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 12.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The former CIA director John Brennan has been subpoenaed to testify next month before a Florida grand jury as part of a Department of Justice investigation into whether former law enforcement and intelligence officials conspired against Donald Trump , one of his lawyers said Monday. Ken Wainstein, an attorney for Brennan, disclosed in a court filing that prosecutors last Thursday presented him with a subpoena for Brennan to appear before a grand jury in Fort Pierce, Florida, on 15 October. He said he was told that the subpoena relates to a “far-reaching” criminal inquiry examining a loosely defined theory that the government officials who have investigated Trump over the last decade, including over Russia election interference in 2016 and his more recent retention of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago estate, conspired to deprive Trump of his civil rights. The subpoena to Brennan is among a flurry that have been issued in recent weeks. Trump ally resigns from post leading inquiry into alleged conspiracy against president Read more Wainstein said he was informed by a prosecutor that Brennan remains a target in a Washington-based investigation into whether he lied to Congress in 2023, a claim the former CIA director and his attorneys have consistently denied. Subpoenas demanding testimony before a grand jury in that false statements probe were issued in spring, then abruptly withdrawn in favor of voluntary interviews. The subpoena was delivered on the same day that Joe diGenova, the prosecutor who had been leading what is casually known as the “grand conspiracy” investigation, abruptly resigned amid what a person familiar with the matter has described as displeasure from the justice department and White House over the pace and management of the investigation. The justice department has not publicly announced a replacement for diGenova. The member of the investigative team with whom Wainstein spoke was Kurt Olsen, a lawyer who unsuccessfully pushed the justice department in 2020 to back the Trump’s false claims that the 2020 election had been stolen from him. The subpoena was disclosed hours ahead of a court hearing in Washington in a lawsuit brought by Brennan. The former CIA director is seeking a court order that would require the preservation of all records from the investigations targeting him, saying such documents would be essential for him to challenge any potential indictment on vindictive prosecution grounds.
